column4: The declaration that human efforts are diverse introduces the two opposed courses whose second end is the blazing fire of 92:14.
Giving and being mindful of God begin the successful course, the specific behavioral opposite of the miserly self-sufficiency that leads toward the warning-fire.
Affirming the finest promise is the opposite response to the denial in 92:9 and 92:16, marking the fork before fire.
God eases the giver toward ease, the other destination set against being eased toward hardship and warned of flame.
Abraham's people propose burning him, but God saves him from the fire; one ayah turns intended fiery confinement into rescue and a sign.
The persecutors command one another to burn Abraham and support their gods, supplying the human punitive intention that God's command to the fire reverses in 21:69.
God makes night a garment and sleep repose, then makes day a rising; covering darkness and rest meet in one formulation behind the section's night-side fire.
Faces are covered as if by pieces of dark night and their owners are companions of the Fire, joining night as covering directly to fiery confinement.
The Book brings people from darknesses into light by God's permission and onto His path, explicitly joining illumination to route-guidance.
A light and clarifying Book are said to have come from God; 5:16 then states that God guides by it along paths of peace.
God guides the human being to the way, leaving a grateful or ungrateful response; the next ayah gives the ungrateful response its fire consequence.
Chains, shackles, and a Blaze are prepared for the ungrateful, turning rejection of the shown way in 76:3 into both enclosure and fire.
Each group thrown into Hell is asked by its keepers whether a warner came, making ignored warning the immediate issue inside the fire scene.
They admit that a warner came but they denied him, supplying the rejected guidance behind their acknowledgment in 67:10.
The أصحاب الأخدود are identified by a fire full of fuel, establishing the trench-fire witnessed in the following ayat.
The persecutors sit over the fuel-filled fire, a spatial reversal of fire closing over its inhabitants.
They witness what they do to the believers, placing culpable human sight beside the fire and sharply answering the supposition that no one sees.
Wealth and children cannot avail the disbelievers against God, and they become fuel for the Fire; presumed protection becomes the material of punishment.
Disbelievers spend wealth to block God's way, then suffer regret, defeat, and gathering into Hell; wealth used against the path ends in fire.
Neither wealth nor children avail their owners against God, and those owners are companions of the Fire, repeating the wealth-to-fire reversal.
The command to seize and shackle the condemned person begins the physical enclosure that continues through Hell in 69:31 and the long chain in 69:32.
The command to bind him in a chain of seventy cubits gives structural force to the confinement surrounding the fire sentence.
The people of Saqar confess that they denied the Day of Judgment, another precise form of the denial that turns a warning into fire.
Failure to urge feeding the poor is named before Hell is brought forward in 89:23, tying the visible fire to refusal of surah 90's ascent.
Consuming inheritance greedily adds a concrete misuse of property to the conduct judged when Hell is brought near.
Excessive love of wealth completes the wealth-centered failure immediately before the judgment scene and the brought-near Hell.
After Hell is brought forward, no one punishes as God punishes; this reverses the human supposition that no one has power over him.
No one binds as God binds, giving the enclosing consequence of the false confidence answered in 89:25.
“Does he not know that God sees?” directly answers the arrogant supposition that no one sees, making divine sight the warning before seizure.
At the reached fire God identifies Himself and commands worship and prayer for remembrance, giving concrete content to the guidance Moses hoped to find there.
The voice at the fire identifies its speaker as God, the Mighty and Wise, completing the transition from a perceived roadside fire to revelation.
Faces are turned about in the Fire while its people wish they had obeyed God and the Messenger; rejected direction becomes bodily exposure to flame.
They say they obeyed leaders who led them away from the path, supplying the misdirection whose fire consequence appears in 33:66.
The people in punishment ask their Lord to bring them out and promise not to return to wrongdoing, directly voicing a desired exit.
God orders them to remain despised in it and not speak, closing the requested exit of 23:107.
Hell has seven gates with an apportioned group for each, giving the punitive destination an explicit bounded architecture.
The addressees will surely see Hellfire, reversing the earlier failure to perceive the warning before it becomes punishment.
They will see it with the eye of certainty, making unavoidable direct sight the final counterpart to a distant sign that could once be followed.
When they see the promised punishment brought near, the disbelievers' faces are distressed; what was treated as remote becomes an immediate visible threat.
Transgression begins the course whose destination is identified as Hell in 79:39.
Preferring the nearer life specifies the choice that makes Hell the refuge in the next ayah.
Hell is the refuge for the one who transgressed and preferred the nearer life, turning a chosen orientation into a final dwelling.
The voice at the reached fire identifies the sacred valley of Tuwa, showing that the distant fire has led Moses to a marked sacred place.
The garden owner doubts the Hour and expects an even better return, extending the false estimate that the sky-sent ḥusbān overturns.
Night is made a garment, another compact Quranic statement of the darkness that covers what the road traveler must discern.
Moses is commanded to bring his people from darknesses into light and remind them of God's days, joining his mission to illumination and remembrance.
God sends clear signs to bring people from darknesses into light, restating the directional work performed by illumination.
One whose breast God opens is upon light from his Lord, while hard hearts are in manifest error; received light and refusal divide into opposed conditions.
A piercing flame pursues the one who snatches a hearing, giving an elevated visible flame a punitive rather than guiding function.
God commands that every stubborn disbeliever be cast into Hell, beginning a short judgment scene whose next ayah names refusal of good.
The person cast into Hell is a preventer of good, linking the fire sentence to obstruction of the good course.
The disbelievers are told to enter Hell's gates and remain there, making the gate a one-way boundary into lasting abode.
The criminals remain perpetually in Hell's punishment, another formulation of the section's exitless closure.
The punishment is not lightened and they are left in despair, specifying the unrelieved condition of the confinement in 43:74.
The disbelievers' fire neither ends in death nor is lightened, making the closed destination temporally as well as spatially inescapable.
